title: Should Politics Drive Your Portfolio Decisions? | Dimensional
gist: Ahead of the 2026 US midterms, Dimensional argues investors should not reposition portfolios based on which party wins Congress: S&P 500 data from 1926 to 2025 show stocks trended upward under Democratic, Republican and mixed control with no reliable partisan pattern. Because markets are forward looking and election expectations are priced in before votes are cast, the authors recommend discipline, diversification and sticking to a long-term plan rather than election-driven trades.

themes.theme: No partisan pattern in US equity returns

insights.claim: Nearly a century of US data (1926-2025) shows no reliable pattern linking Democratic, Republican or split control of Congress to better or worse stock market returns.
insights.speaker: Isabelle Williams
insights.so_what: Partisan-control-based sector or beta tilts lack historical support as a systematic signal.
insights.quote: Nearly a century of data shows no reliable pattern linking any political party’s control of Congress to better or worse stock market returns.

insights.claim: From 1926 to 2025, as measured by growth of $1 in the S&P 500 Index, stocks trended upward under Democratic majorities, Republican majorities and periods of mixed congressional control alike.

insights.so_what: Staying invested through any political configuration has historically captured the long-run equity uptrend.

themes.theme: Why elections are a poor trading signal

insights.claim: Election results are only one of many forces on stock prices, alongside inflation, interest rates, economic growth, technological innovation and geopolitical events, which move markets every day.
insights.speaker: Isabelle Williams
insights.so_what: Macro and rate drivers are likely to swamp any party-control effect, so positioning should be anchored on those rather than on vote outcomes.
insights.quote: Inflation, interest rates, economic growth, technological innovation, geopolitical events, and countless other variables influence market prices every day.

insights.claim: Because markets are forward looking, expectations about election outcomes are reflected in prices long before votes are cast, so much of the information is already priced by the time results are known.
insights.speaker: Isabelle Williams
insights.so_what: Trading on a consensus election outcome after the fact offers little edge; only genuine surprises carry new information.
insights.quote: Expectations about election outcomes are reflected in prices long before any votes are cast.

insights.claim: Although elections undoubtedly matter, the evidence suggests they are unlikely to give investors a reliable road map for portfolio decisions; staying disciplined, diversified and on a long-term financial plan is the better course than trying to outguess markets.
insights.speaker: Isabelle Williams
insights.so_what: Expect Dimensional-style advisors to counsel clients against midterm-driven allocation changes, dampening retail flow volatility around the vote.
